title: The Grace of Giving: The Collection for Jerusalem
summary: Paul holds up the churches of Macedonia, who in deep poverty and severe trial begged to share in the relief offering for the believers in Jerusalem. He urges the Corinthians to finish the collection they began a year earlier, grounding his appeal in the grace of Christ, who though rich became poor for their sake, and in the principle of equality illustrated by the manna in the wilderness. He then commends Titus and two trusted brothers who will handle the gift, taking care that everything is done honorably before God and people.
story: With the relationship between Paul and the Corinthians repaired (chapter 7), Paul turns to unfinished business. For several years he had been organizing a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor believers of Jerusalem. The Corinthians had been among the first to commit to it (verse 10; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4), but during the troubles of the past year their giving had stalled. Chapters 8 and 9 are Paul's appeal to complete it. The collection was carried to Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary trip (Romans 15:25-28; Acts 24:17), where Paul was arrested, so the gift these chapters prepare stands near the end of the story Acts tells of his free ministry.
historical:
The Jerusalem church had faced poverty for years. Acts records famine relief sent from Antioch in the 40s (Acts 11:27-30), and when the Jerusalem leaders recognized Paul's mission to the Gentiles, they asked him only to "remember the poor", which he says he was eager to do (Galatians 2:10). Causes may have included famine, the economic pressure on believers excluded from family and synagogue support, and the large number of widows and poor in the early community (Acts 6:1).

The collection meant more to Paul than relief. In Romans 15:26-27 he explains that the Gentile churches owe a debt to Jerusalem: if they have shared in the Jews' spiritual blessings, they should share their material goods. The gift was a visible sign that Jewish and Gentile believers were one church. The Macedonian churches (Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea) were poor and had suffered persecution from the start (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14; Philippians 1:29-30), which makes their eagerness striking. Some scholars, notably Hans Dieter Betz, have argued that chapters 8 and 9 were originally separate administrative letters; others read them as a single appeal in two parts.
cultural:
Giving in the Greek and Roman world usually ran through patronage. A wealthy benefactor funded a building or a festival and received public honor, inscriptions, and loyalty in return; a gift created an obligation. Paul reframes giving entirely. He calls the gift charis, grace, the same word he uses for God's free kindness in Christ, and describes it with words like service, fellowship, and blessing. He avoids the ordinary vocabulary of money altogether. Giving becomes a response to grace received, not a way to purchase status.

Handling money across long distances also invited suspicion. Travelling teachers were often accused of greed, and Paul had refused support from the Corinthians partly for that reason (11:7-12). So he arranges for the funds to be carried not by himself alone but by delegates, including a brother "chosen by the churches" (verse 19), so that no one can accuse him of misusing the gift. Verse 21 echoes Proverbs 3:4 in the Greek translation: to do what is right before the Lord and before people.
literary: The chapter moves from example to appeal to arrangements. Verses 1-5 tell the story of the Macedonians, told as "the grace that God has given" them, so that their generosity is presented as God's work. Verses 6-15 are the appeal, carefully tactful: Paul says he is not commanding (verse 8) but offering advice (verse 10), and he builds on the Corinthians' own earlier eagerness. At the center stands verse 9, a compressed statement of the gospel in economic terms. Verses 13-15 argue for equality and quote Exodus 16:18, where each Israelite gathered manna and no one had too much or too little. Verses 16-24 read like a letter of recommendation for Titus and the two unnamed brothers. The word charis appears seven times in the chapter with a range of meanings: grace, gift, act of kindness, and thanks.

outline.t: The example of the Macedonian churches
Excel in this grace of giving
The grace of Christ: rich, yet he became poor
Finish what you began: the principle of equality
Titus and the brothers commended; care for integrity

doctrines.note: Verse 9 describes salvation as an exchange: Christ "was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich". The riches are spiritual (reconciliation, adoption, new life), and they are given, not earned. Generous giving flows from having received this.

The collection bound Gentile churches in Greece to the Jewish church in Jerusalem. Paul's principle of equality (verses 13-14) describes a church whose members across distance and ethnicity share one another's needs, not as charity from above but as mutual belonging.

Paul takes "great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men" (verse 21). The integrity of how money is handled is part of the church's witness; carelessness can discredit the gospel itself.

words.note: Charis, grace. Its basic sense is favor freely given, and from there it can mean a gift, an act of kindness, or gratitude. Paul uses it for God's grace to the Macedonians (verse 1), for the collection itself (verses 6-7, 19), for Christ's self-giving (verse 9), and for thanks to God (verse 16). The repetition teaches that human generosity is grace passed on.

Koinonia, fellowship, sharing, participation. In verse 4 the BSB renders it "the privilege of sharing". The word describes partnership in something held in common, and it can refer to a financial contribution (Romans 15:26). Giving is a form of fellowship.

Isotes, equality or fairness. Paul does not mean that everyone must have identical possessions, but that surplus in one place should meet need in another, so that no one is crushed while others have excess. The manna story (verse 15) is his model.

Ptocheuo, to become poor, to be reduced to poverty; the related noun ptochos describes the destitute beggar. It appears only here in the New Testament, describing Christ's self-emptying in the incarnation and the cross.

christ: Verse 9 is one of the New Testament's great summaries of what Christ has done: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich." It assumes that Christ existed in riches before he became human, which Philippians 2:6-8 describes as being in the form of God and emptying himself to take the form of a servant. His poverty includes his birth into a humble family, his life without a home of his own, and above all his death. Paul makes this the pattern and motive for giving: the church gives because it has been given to, and it gives in the shape of Christ's own self-giving.
questions: The Macedonians gave out of deep poverty and saw giving as a privilege. What keeps people who have more from giving as freely as people who have less?
Paul roots generosity in Christ becoming poor for our sake rather than in guilt or duty. How would that change the way a church talks about money?
Paul arranges trustworthy people and transparent handling of the gift. What practices protect the integrity of churches and ministries with money today?
